subject: Cloud Computing
title: SaaS: Software You Rent
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: SaaS: Software You Rent.

hook.text: Gmail, Slack, Zoom, Notion — you use them daily but never installed any of them on a server.

buildup.text: SaaS delivers complete applications over the internet. You pay a subscription and just use them.

discovery.text: The provider handles everything: servers, security, updates, backups. You just log in and work.

twist.text: SaaS is a $200 billion market. The average company uses over 100 different SaaS applications.

climax.text: SaaS turned software from a product you buy once into a subscription you pay forever.

punchline.text: SaaS: you never own it. You just keep paying for it.

quiz.question: What defines SaaS compared to other cloud models?
options: The provider delivers a complete application — the customer just uses it
Customers install the software on their own cloud servers
SaaS only works on mobile devices, not computers

details.summary: SaaS delivers complete applications over the internet on a subscription basis. Users access software through a browser without installing, updating, or maintaining anything. Gmail, Salesforce, Slack, and Zoom are all SaaS products used by billions.
details.whyItMatters: SaaS has become the default software delivery model. Understanding it explains how modern businesses consume and pay for the tools they use daily.
takeaways: SaaS delivers ready-to-use software via the browser
Users pay subscriptions instead of buying licenses
Updates and maintenance are handled by the provider

faq.question: How does SaaS differ from traditional software?
faq.answer: Traditional software requires purchase, installation, and local maintenance. SaaS runs in the cloud, accessed via browser, with automatic updates and pay-as-you-go pricing. No hardware or IT staff is needed to deploy or maintain SaaS applications.

faq.question: Who manages SaaS security?
faq.answer: The SaaS provider manages infrastructure and application security. Customers are responsible for user access management, data they upload, and configuring available security settings like MFA. The shared responsibility model still applies but with a smaller customer scope.
